question.text: In an HIV-positive patient on saquinavir-based ART, does habitual garlic supplementation (>4 g/day aged garlic extract) reduce protease-inhibitor plasma concentrations sufficiently to risk virologic failure?

support: Pharmacokinetic studies in HIV-positive patients have shown that aged garlic extract (AGE) at doses >4 g/day can induce CYP3A4 activity, leading to a 30–50% reduction in plasma concentrations of protease inhibitors such as saquinavir.

A randomized crossover trial reported that participants taking 5 g/day of AGE experienced a significant decrease in saquinavir AUC and trough levels, falling below the therapeutic threshold associated with virologic suppression.
Guidelines on drug–herb interactions list garlic as a moderate inducer of CYP3A4 and advise monitoring of protease inhibitor levels when high-dose garlic supplements are used.
concerns: The magnitude of the interaction varies between individuals; some patients may maintain adequate drug levels despite garlic supplementation, making risk assessment uncertain.
Most available studies are short-term (≤2 weeks) and involve small sample sizes, limiting the ability to predict long-term virologic outcomes such as failure or resistance development.
Garlic's effect on other antiretroviral agents (e.g., ritonavir-boosted regimens) is less well characterized, so extrapolation to all protease inhibitors may be inappropriate.
verdicts.notes: High-dose garlic supplementation can meaningfully lower saquinavir plasma concentrations, potentially compromising virologic control. Clinicians should monitor drug levels or advise patients to avoid >4 g/day of aged garlic extract while on saquinavir-based ART.
